title: Seasonal growth in fish and man follows a damped sine curve

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Seasonal growth in fish and man follows a damped sine curve

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: In fishes such as plaice and haddock, and in man, growth is slower in winter than in summer, as if an annual sine curve were superimposed on the growth curve, and the amplitude of this fluctuation dies away as growth slows, giving a damped sine curve.

fields.label: Notation
fields.value: L(t) = \bar{L}(t) + A(t)\sin(2\pi t / 1\,\text{yr}), A(t) \to 0 as d\bar{L}/dt \to 0 (damped sine)

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: in short, our phenomenon is simply expressed by what is known as a “damped sine-curve.” Exactly the same thing occurs in man, though neither in his case nor in that of the fish have we sufficient data for its complete illustration.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter III, “The Rate of Growth”; topic “Seasonal fluctuations of growth”. Scope: fishes (plaice, haddock) and humans

fields.label: Notation
fields.value: L(t) = \bar{L}(t) + A(t)\sin(2\pi t / 1\,\text{yr}), A(t) \to 0 as d\bar{L}/dt \to 0 (damped sine)

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch03-23: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.64

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Seasonality and damping have direct statistical meanings and can be compared with nonperiodic growth models. Existing fish data can test population-level patterns, but the full claim needs longitudinal, seasonally resolved measurements in both fishes and humans.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Fit longitudinal length or mass trajectories with and without an annually periodic term whose amplitude declines with age, separately in plaice, haddock, and humans. Support requires improved out-of-sample fit and declining seasonal amplitude in each stated group.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Cross-sectional fish surveys do not track the same individuals.

Open human longitudinal records with fine seasonal resolution are limited.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
discriminating power: 0.75
data existence: 0.55
operationalizability: 0.85
analysis feasibility: 0.7
data adequacy: 0.4

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The fish half of the claim can be tested with open age-length surveys timed through the year, and damping is a sharp extra prediction beyond 'growth is seasonal'. Those surveys still do not follow individuals, and the human half still lacks a public longitudinal counterpart to Daffner's cadet table. The claim is therefore testable for North Sea plaice and haddock, and only weakly for humans.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Fit seasonal increments of length or stature to a sine term whose amplitude declines as mean growth rate declines. A winter deficit that shrinks smoothly toward zero with age would support the damped-sine description; irregular seasonality, or an amplitude that does not damp, would refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Temperature, feeding and day length move together, so a pure annual sine is not isolated.

Open human series rarely repeat the same individuals at half-year intervals across adolescence.

Survey lengths are cross-sectional, so size-selective mortality is mixed with growth.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:

analysis feasibility: 0.65
data existence: 0.6
operationalizability: 0.75
data adequacy: 0.45
